idiom_name: centralized exit: acquire, funnel every failure path through one cleanup label; __attribute__((cleanup(fn))) where the compiler allows it
implementation_notes: C has neither destructors nor a scope-exit statement, so the classic owner object is replaced by a convention: acquire the handle, jump to a single cleanup label from every failure path, release in reverse acquisition order and empty the handle so the shared exit stays idempotent (the Linux kernel's coding style documents exactly this centralized-exit shape). GCC and Clang add the cleanup attribute (__attribute__((cleanup(fn))) or, in C23 attribute syntax, [[gnu::cleanup(fn)]]), which runs fn when an automatic variable leaves scope and is the closest thing C has to real RAII; it is a compiler extension rather than ISO C, so portable code keeps the goto form and every reviewer checks the single exit. Both forms need the same discipline: one owner per handle, release exactly once, and a cleanup function that tolerates an empty handle.
pitfalls: The cleanup label is a convention, not a guarantee: a later edit that adds an early return above it (or a break out of a loop) skips the release silently, and the leak shows up only on the failure path that was added.

The cleanup attribute runs its function on every scope exit, so the variable must be initialised to a safe empty handle (NULL, -1) before any early jump and the cleanup function must tolerate that value; an uninitialized automatic makes the compiler run the destructor on garbage.
Releasing a handle twice (fclose/free after the explicit path already ran, or a shared exit reached from two owners) is undefined behaviour: exactly one owner per handle and one release point.
